newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan prosecutors question more DKB executives.
newsitem.headline: Japan prosecutors question more DKB executives.

text.p: In the latest twist to Japan's unfolding financial scandal, prosecutors on Tuesday questioned executives from Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd as the bank unveiled a sweeping management shake-up, its second in less than a month.

Japanese media said prosecutors were questioning Ichiro Fujita, a vice president who had been expected to become president later this month, as well as other former and current executives, in connection with an affair involving payoffs to a racketeer that has already ensnared Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

The scandal, which has so far led to the arrests of 10 people, including four DKB officials and a former Nomura president, is unfolding just as Japan kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms of its long-protected financial sector -- a fact which has made authorities keen to take a tough stance.

The fresh moves by prosecutors, which domestic media said reflected a growing suspicion that top DKB management was involved in the scandal, came as the bank announced a new executive line-up which it said was untainted by the affair.

Public outrage over the scandal has already forced DKB, Japan's second biggest bank in terms of deposits, to scrap initial plans for a management reshuffle which would have promoted Fujita to the post of president.
Fujita has admitted that he knew of the bank's loans to Yoshinori Koike, the younger brother of Ryuichi Koike, the "sokaiya" racketeer at the heart of the scandal.
DKB said on Tuesday that managing director Katsuyuki Sugita, 54, would take over as president on June 27.
Twenty-one of the bank's 40 directors, including chairman Tadashi Okuda, president Katsuhiko Kondo and Fujita, will step down altogether.
Okuda and Kondo were to resign their posts in the first reshuffle plan, but would have stayed at the bank as advisers.

"It is extremely regrettable that the scandal has lowered our credibility as a bank and as a company," DKB said. "We selected individuals who had not been detected to have any involvement in the scandal in our internal investigations."

DKB, which like Nomura is suffering customer defections and faces possible stiff administrative penalties over the scandal, said it would implement management reforms to prevent any future misdeeds, including the creation of a committee of outside auditors to check for dubious business activities.

Japan's Commercial Code bans payoffs to sokaiya, who extort money from firms by threatening to disrupt shareholders meetings. But many firms have found it tough to cut the ties that bind them to the underworld.

The affair is the second to involve Nomura since a 1991 brokerage scandal, when then-chairman Setsuya Tabuchi and president Yoshihisa Tabuchi (no relation) left their posts after revelations that the firm had ties to gangsters and had improperly compensated favoured clients.

Now Nomura has been indicted for violating the securities law by illegally compensating a firm run by Yoshinori Koike, and two former Nomura directors have been indicted for violating the securities law and Commercial Code. Former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki was arrested last week and the two Tabuchi's have reportedly been questioned by prosecutors.
Nomura has already effected its own broad management reshuffle, promoting Junichi Unjiie, a 51-year-old corporate youngster with a University of Chicago doctorate, to president.
Authorities are widely believed to want to make an example of the two firms to teach others a lesson in corporate ethics and to clean up the financial sector's image ahead of deregulation.
But some experts say the old ways cannot be completely erased unless and until much of the current generation of top executives at financial institutions relinquishes power.
"We're dealing with an entire generation who has to go into retirement before conduct really changes," one financial industry source said.
